claim: γ-Secretase is a multi-subunit enzyme whose aberrant activity is associated with Alzheimer's disease and cancer.
source: γ-Secretase is a multi-subunit enzyme whose aberrant activity is associated with Alzheimer's disease and cancer.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, representing general scientific knowledge about γ-secretase.

claim: The γ-secretase complex is formed by the catalytic presenilin (PSEN), nicastrin (NCT), anterior-pharynx defective 1 (APH1) and presenilin enhancer 2 (PEN2).
source: The γ-secretase complex is an intramembrane cleaving protease (i-CLiP) formed by the catalytic presenilin (PSEN), nicastrin (NCT), anterior-pharynx defective 1 (APH1) and presenilin enhancer 2 (PEN2) (De Strooper, 2003; Kimberly et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to De Strooper, 2003 and Kimberly et al., 2003.

claim: γ-Secretase cleaves more than a hundred type-I transmembrane substrates.
source: It cleaves more than a hundred type-I transmembrane substrates (Jurisch-Yaksi et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citation to Jurisch-Yaksi et al., 2013.

claim: γ-Secretase substrates include Notch, ErbB4, and the Amyloid Precursor Protein (APP).
source: It cleaves more than a hundred type-I transmembrane substrates (Jurisch-Yaksi et al., 2013) including Notch (important for development and cancer), ErbB4 (involved in breast cancer), and the Amyloid Precursor Protein (APP), whose cleavage product is the toxic amyloid-β, a major hallmark in Alzheimer's disease (Annaert and De Strooper, 2002; Selkoe and Hardy, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jurisch-Yaksi et al., 2013; Annaert and De Strooper, 2002; Selkoe and Hardy, 2016.

claim: The γ-secretase complex is assembled in a 1:1:1:1 ratio.
source: The complex is assembled in a 1:1:1:1 ratio (Sato et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citation to Sato et al., 2007.

claim: γ-Secretase complex assembly is thought to be mediated through recycling from the Golgi to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER).
source: The complex is assembled in a 1:1:1:1 ratio (Sato et al., 2007) in early biosynthetic compartments, a process thought to be mediated through recycling from the Golgi to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) (Spasic et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Spasic et al., 2007 and described as 'thought to be', indicating inference from prior work.

claim: Overexpression of any γ-secretase subunit results in its ER jamming.
source: Whereas overexpression of any subunit results in its ER jamming, the knock-out (KO) of a single subunit prevents complex assembly and destabilizes remaining subunits, all together underscoring that all are required for complex assembly (Steiner et al., 2002; Luo et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Steiner et al., 2002 and Luo et al., 2003.

claim: The knock-out of a single γ-secretase subunit prevents complex assembly and destabilizes remaining subunits.
source: Whereas overexpression of any subunit results in its ER jamming, the knock-out (KO) of a single subunit prevents complex assembly and destabilizes remaining subunits, all together underscoring that all are required for complex assembly (Steiner et al., 2002; Luo et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Steiner et al., 2002 and Luo et al., 2003.

claim: A mature functional γ-secretase complex is characterized by glycosylated NCT.
source: A mature functional γ-secretase complex is characterized by glycosylated NCT (Yu et al., 2000) and the endoproteolysis and heterodimerization of PSEN N- and C-termini (Luo et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yu et al., 2000 and Luo et al., 2003.

claim: A mature functional γ-secretase complex is characterized by the endoproteolysis and heterodimerization of PSEN N- and C-termini.
source: A mature functional γ-secretase complex is characterized by glycosylated NCT (Yu et al., 2000) and the endoproteolysis and heterodimerization of PSEN N- and C-termini (Luo et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Luo et al., 2003.

claim: The mature form of γ-secretase is long-lived as opposed to unassembled subunits that are rapidly degraded.
source: This form is long-lived as opposed to unassembled subunits that are rapidly degraded (De Strooper and Annaert, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to De Strooper and Annaert, 2010.

claim: γ-Secretase protein structure has been unveiled at atomic resolution.
source: While enormous progress has been made in the past years to unveil γ-secretase protein structure at atomic resolution (Bai et al., 2015b)
evidence: Supported by citation to Bai et al., 2015b.

claim: There is a lack of direct evidence to reveal γ-secretase distribution and dynamics in membranes of living cells.
source: While enormous progress has been made in the past years to unveil γ-secretase protein structure at atomic resolution (Bai et al., 2015b), we are still lacking direct evidence to reveal γ-secretase distribution and dynamics in membranes of living cells.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field prior to this study.

claim: FLIM-FRET and molecular dynamics simulations have helped to better understand conformational changes γ-secretase undergoes for substrate recognition and cleaving mechanisms.
source: Only microscopy techniques like FLIM-FRET and molecular dynamics simulations based on the γ-secretase 3D-cryo structure have helped to better understand conformational changes γ-secretase undergoes for substrate recognition and cleaving mechanisms (Wolfe, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wolfe, 2019.

claim: Lipidome analysis of immunoprecipitated γ-secretase identified cholesterol and phosphatidylcholine molecules.
source: Lipidome analysis of immunoprecipitated γ-secretase identified cholesterol and phosphatidylcholine molecules, which were also identified in γ-secretase 3D-cryo structures (Yang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang et al., 2019.

claim: Cholesterol and phosphatidylcholine molecules were identified in γ-secretase 3D-cryo structures.
source: Lipidome analysis of immunoprecipitated γ-secretase identified cholesterol and phosphatidylcholine molecules, which were also identified in γ-secretase 3D-cryo structures (Yang et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang et al., 2019.

claim: Most data on γ-secretase association with lipid rafts rely on the biochemical characterization of detergent-resistant membranes and flotation gradient centrifugation.
source: However, to date, most of these data rely on the biochemical characterization of detergent-resistant membranes and flotation gradient centrifugation (Vetrivel et al., 2004; Hur et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Vetrivel et al., 2004 and Hur et al., 2008.

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation and gel filtration approaches found γ-secretase associated with high molecular weight, up to megadalton, complexes that include the cognate sheddases, ADAM10 and BACE1.
source: Likewise, co-immunoprecipitation and gel filtration approaches found γ-secretase associated with high molecular weight, up to megadalton, complexes that include the cognate sheddases, ADAM10 and BACE1 (Chen et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2015 and Liu et al., 2019.

claim: The lateral nanoscale organization of γ-secretase has not been corroborated with imaging approaches due to the lack of resolution.
source: However, this lateral nanoscale organization of γ-secretase has thus far not been corroborated with imaging approaches for long because of the lack of resolution.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of prior imaging approaches.

claim: Conventional widefield and confocal microscopy are limited to ~200 nm lateral resolution.
source: Given the diffraction limit of light, conventional widefield and confocal microscopy are limited to ~200 nm lateral resolution.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the diffraction limit of light microscopy.

claim: Super-resolution microscopy has increased lateral resolution up to ~100 nm for SIM and ~20 nm for STED and SMLM.
source: Thanks to Structured Illumination Microscopy (SIM), Stimulated Emission Depletion (STED) microscopy and Single-Molecule Localization Microscopy (SMLM), the lateral resolution has been increased up to ~100 nm for SIM and ~20 nm for STED and SMLM.
evidence: This is established knowledge about super-resolution microscopy techniques.

claim: The study combined SIM, molecular counting by photobleaching and sptPALM to advance the current biochemical knowledge on γ-secretase.
source: In this study, we combined SIM, molecular counting by photobleaching (Ulbrich and Isacoff, 2007; Arant and Ulbrich, 2014) and sptPALM to advance the current biochemical knowledge on γ-secretase.
evidence: This describes the methodological approach of the study, with citations for the techniques.

claim: PSEN1/γ-secretase complexes are particularly abundant at the plasma membrane.
source: We focus on PSEN1/γ-secretase complexes not only for their relevance for the Alzheimer's disease and cancer (Haapasalo and Kovacs, 2011; Jurisch-Yaksi et al., 2013; Voytyuk et al., 2018), but also because it is particularly abundant at the PM making it more accessible to different microscopy techniques (Sannerud et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sannerud et al., 2016.

claim: The study shows PSEN1/γ-secretase stoichiometry at the PM at single-molecule resolution for the first time.
source: We show for the first time PSEN1/γ-secretase stoichiometry at the PM at single-molecule resolution
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the experimental data presented.

claim: PSEN1/γ-secretase has a majorly mono- and dimeric distribution in living cells.
source: We show for the first time PSEN1/γ-secretase stoichiometry at the PM at single-molecule resolution and provide evidence of its majorly mono- and dimeric distribution in living cells.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: sptPALM identified dynamic hotspots where PSEN1/γ-secretase is recruited.
source: sptPALM identified dynamic hotspots where PSEN1/γ-secretase is recruited, which are influenced by γ-secretase inhibitor (GSI) treatments
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: PSEN1/γ-secretase hotspots are influenced by γ-secretase inhibitor (GSI) treatments.
source: sptPALM identified dynamic hotspots where PSEN1/γ-secretase is recruited, which are influenced by γ-secretase inhibitor (GSI) treatments
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: The study visualized γ-secretase association with substrates like amyloid precursor protein and N-cadherin at the cell surface.
source: We visualized γ-secretase association with substrates like amyloid precursor protein and N-cadherin, but not with its sheddases ADAM10 or BACE1 at the cell surface
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: The study did not visualize γ-secretase association with its sheddases ADAM10 or BACE1 at the cell surface.
source: We visualized γ-secretase association with substrates like amyloid precursor protein and N-cadherin, but not with its sheddases ADAM10 or BACE1 at the cell surface
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the experimental data presented in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The study's results argue against pre-formed megadalton complexes of γ-secretase with sheddases.
source: We visualized γ-secretase association with substrates like amyloid precursor protein and N-cadherin, but not with its sheddases ADAM10 or BACE1 at the cell surface, arguing against pre-formed megadalton complexes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data, representing an inference from the observations.

claim: In living cells, PSEN1/γ-secretase transiently visits ADAM10 hotspots.
source: Nonetheless, in living cells PSEN1/γ-secretase transiently visits ADAM10 hotspots.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by the experimental data presented in Figure 5.

claim: GFP or mEOS3.2 tags on PSEN1 and SNAP-tag on NCT do not interfere with complex assembly and maturation.
source: To ensure that the introduced tags did not interfere with complex assembly and maturation, we first tested each of them in single KO backgrounds. For both, PSEN1 endoproteolysis and mature glycosylation of NCT was observed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B), as well as broad localization in different subcellular compartments (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C). This underscores that the introduced tags do not interfere with normal maturation of subunits and complex formation
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B,C.

claim: The introduced tags on PSEN1 and NCT are in agreement with previous reports on PSEN and NCT tagging.
source: This underscores that the introduced tags do not interfere with normal maturation of subunits and complex formation, which is in agreement with previous reports on PSEN and NCT tagging (Kaether et al., 2006; Cui et al., 2015; Sannerud et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kaether et al., 2006; Cui et al., 2015; Sannerud et al., 2016.

claim: A triple KO (tKO; NCT-/-, PSEN1-/-, PSEN2-/-) mouse embryonic fibroblast (MEF) cell line was engineered using CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing.
source: For the single-molecule visualization of both tagged subunits in one γ-secretase complex in situ, we next engineered a triple KO (tKO; NCT-/-, PSEN1-/-, PSEN2-/-) mouse embryonic fibroblast (MEF) cell line using CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing.
evidence: This describes a methodological approach used in the study.

claim: tKO MEFs were stably rescued with NCT-SNAP and GFP-PSEN1 to generate rescued cell lines with two tagged γ-secretase subunits.
source: These tKO MEFs were subsequently used to stably re-introduce NCT-SNAP and GFP-PSEN1 to generate rescued cell lines with two tagged γ-secretase subunits (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes a methodological approach used in the study, with reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Fluorescence-Activated Cell Sorting (FACS) was used to select four populations depending on the relative levels of either PSEN1 or NCT.
source: To obtain balanced levels of both subunits, we labeled NCT-SNAP with the far-red fluorescent cell-permeable SNAP-SiR ligand and used Fluorescence-Activated Cell Sorting (FACS) to select four populations depending on the relative levels of either PSEN1 or NCT (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This describes a methodological approach used in the study, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Population P8 had the highest levels of mature glycosylated NCT-SNAP and PSEN1 heterodimers.
source: We selected P8 for further experiments, which (i) had the highest levels of mature glycosylated NCT-SNAP and PSEN1 heterodimers
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Population P8 exhibited no apparent accumulations of full-length PSEN1.
source: We selected P8 for further experiments, which (i) had the highest levels of mature glycosylated NCT-SNAP and PSEN1 heterodimers, but (ii) exhibited no apparent accumulations of full-length PSEN1 (indicating non-incorporation into complexes)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Population P8 showed PEN2 stabilization.
source: We selected P8 for further experiments, which (i) had the highest levels of mature glycosylated NCT-SNAP and PSEN1 heterodimers, but (ii) exhibited no apparent accumulations of full-length PSEN1 (indicating non-incorporation into complexes), (iii) showed PEN2 stabilization
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Population P8 showed normalized processing of APP-CTF as a direct substrate of γ-secretase.
source: We selected P8 for further experiments, which (i) had the highest levels of mature glycosylated NCT-SNAP and PSEN1 heterodimers, but (ii) exhibited no apparent accumulations of full-length PSEN1 (indicating non-incorporation into complexes), (iii) showed PEN2 stabilization, and (iv) normalized processing of APP-CTF as a direct substrate of γ-secretase (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Blue native PAGE of a 0.5% DDM cell extract displayed the expected ~440 kDa high molecular weight complex.
source: Blue native PAGE of a 0.5% n-Dodecyl β-D-maltoside (DDM) cell extract displayed the expected ~440 kDa high molecular weight complex (HMWC), as previously reported (Kimberly et al., 2003; Fraering et al., 2004) and indicating proper assembly of the tagged subunits into a mature complex (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1F and citations to Kimberly et al., 2003 and Fraering et al., 2004.

claim: Aminolipid-coated superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticles (SPIONs) were used to isolate highly purified plasma membranes.
source: To confirm the presence of mature tagged complexes at the cell surface, we used aminolipid-coated superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticles (SPIONs) to isolate highly purified PMs (Figure 1—figure supplemental 1G; Tharkeshwar et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes a methodological approach used in the study, with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1G and citation to Tharkeshwar et al., 2017.

claim: GFP-PSEN1-NTF co-immunoprecipitated with NCT-SNAP and PSEN1-CTF in ratios similar to those from the input.
source: Subsequent pull-down with GFP antibodies from CHAPSO extracted PMs (which preserves γ-secretase complex integrity), followed by SDS-PAGE and quantitative western blotting showed that GFP-PSEN1-NTF co-immunoprecipitated with NCT-SNAP and PSEN1-CTF in ratios that are similar to those from the input (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Blue native PAGE of DDM-extracted PMs confirmed the integrity of the tagged complex.
source: Blue native PAGE of DDM-extracted PMs further confirmed the integrity of the tagged complex (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Quantitative western blotting gave a GFP-PSEN1/NCT-SNAP ratio in tKO samples comparable to the one observed in WT and single KO (sKO) GFP-PSEN1.
source: Lastly, quantitative western blotting, using recombinant γ-secretase as a standard, gave a GFP-PSEN1/NCT-SNAP ratio in tKO samples comparable to the one observed in WT and single KO (sKO) GFP-PSEN1 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Confocal imaging revealed co-localized subunits at the cell surface, including membrane ruffles.
source: Confocal imaging revealed co-localized subunits at the cell surface, including membrane ruffles (Figure 1E), and in LAMP1-positive organelles (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: The tKO NCT-SNAP/GFP-PSEN1 rescued MEFs demonstrated normal assembly, maturation and localization of the tagged subunits into γ-secretase complexes, indistinguishable from WT cells.
source: Thus, the tKO NCT-SNAP/GFP-PSEN1 rescued MEFs demonstrated a normal assembly, maturation and localization of the tagged subunits into γ-secretase complexes, indistinguishable from WT cells.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data presented in Figure 1 and its supplements.

claim: In the absence of PSEN expression, tKO NCT-SNAP MEFs had a close to 8-fold decreased NCT-SNAP density at the cell surface compared to tKO NCT-SNAP/GFP-PSEN1 MEFs.
source: We next analyzed PM sheets from tKO MEFs rescued with only NCT-SNAP or together with GFP-PSEN1 imaged by SIM. In the absence of PSEN expression, tKO NCT-SNAP MEFs had a close to 8-fold decreased NCT-SNAP density at the cell surface compared to tKO NCT-SNAP/GFP-PSEN1 MEFs (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The trafficking of unassembled subunits is strongly impaired when another subunit is missing.
source: These results demonstrate that the trafficking of unassembled subunits is strongly impaired when another subunit, in this case, PSEN1, is missing further consolidating the normal complex assembly in tKO NCT-SNAP/GFP-PSEN1 MEFs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Most GFP-PSEN1 spots overlap with or adjoin NCT-SNAP-SiR spots in PM sheets from tKO NCT-SNAP-SiR/GFP-PSEN1 MEFs.
source: PM sheets from tKO NCT-SNAP-SiR/GFP-PSEN1 MEFs displayed most GFP-PSEN1 spots overlapping with or adjoining NCT-SNAP-SiR spots (Figure 1H, middle panel).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The density ratio of NCT-SNAP:GFP-PSEN1 was indistinguishable from immunolabeling GFP-PSEN1 with GFPbooster-Atto647N indicating a one to one stoichiometry.
source: The density ratio of NCT-SNAP:GFP-PSEN1 was indistinguishable from immunolabeling GFP-PSEN1 with GFPbooster-Atto647N (GFPnb) indicating a one to one stoichiometry (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Nearest-neighbor analysis revealed a peak at ~50 nm for NCT-SNAP-SiR over GFP-PSEN1.
source: This was confirmed by nearest-neighbor analysis, wherein the distance to the nearest-neighbor is measured starting from the centroid coordinates of the spot. Herein, NCT-SNAP-SiR over GFP-PSEN1 revealed a peak at ~50 nm, that is slightly larger compared to the ~20 nm for GFP-PSEN1 over GFPbooster-Atto647N, but clearly distinct from a theoretical random distribution (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Nearest-neighbor analysis revealed a peak at ~20 nm for GFP-PSEN1 over GFPbooster-Atto647N.
source: This was confirmed by nearest-neighbor analysis, wherein the distance to the nearest-neighbor is measured starting from the centroid coordinates of the spot. Herein, NCT-SNAP-SiR over GFP-PSEN1 revealed a peak at ~50 nm, that is slightly larger compared to the ~20 nm for GFP-PSEN1 over GFPbooster-Atto647N, but clearly distinct from a theoretical random distribution (Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: About 16% for GFPnb and 30% for NCT of the total population follow the random distribution.
source: We noticed a fraction of the experimental population that follows the random distribution in both cases, representing about 16% for GFPnb and 30% for NCT of the total population.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The fraction following random distribution likely corresponds to GFPnb or NCT-SNAP that pair with GFP-PSEN1 of another complex that is not visible.
source: These likely correspond to GFPnb or NCT-SNAP that pair with GFP-PSEN1 of another complex that is not visible, either due to GFP photobleaching or immature chromophores.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data, representing an inference.

claim: The expected fraction of fluorescent GFP at the PM for a given GFP construct is ~80%.
source: Indeed, the expected fraction of fluorescent GFP at the PM for a given GFP construct is ~80%, which is in line with our observed association to GFPnb or NCT-SNAP by GFP-PSEN1 (Ulbrich and Isacoff, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ulbrich and Isacoff, 2007.

claim: The resolution of SIM is limited to 100 nm.
source: As the resolution of SIM is limited to 100 nm, distances up to 100 nm are considered associations.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the resolution of SIM.

claim: The slightly higher paired distance for PSEN1-NCT compared to the dual-labeled GFP-PSEN1 may originate from the linkers used to fuse the SNAP-tag and GFP to NCT and PSEN1.
source: The slightly higher paired distance for PSEN1-NCT compared to the dual-labeled GFP-PSEN1 may originate from the linkers used to fuse the SNAP-tag and GFP to NCT and PSEN1, respectively. Theoretically, they separate the tags to a maximum of ~60 nm (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data, representing speculation about the cause of the observed distance.

claim: The close apposition/co-localization of NCT and PSEN1 at the PM confirms the biochemical predicted 1:1 ratio in γ-secretase complexes.
source: Thus, the close apposition/co-localization of NCT and PSEN1 at the PM of fully rescued tKO MEFs confirms the biochemical predicted 1:1 ratio in γ-secretase complexes.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: NCT-PSEN1 spots likely correspond to one fluorophore each, thus representing one γ-secretase complex per spot.
source: As NCT-PSEN1 spots had almost a 1:1 ratio in a very short distance range (<50 nm), these spots likely correspond to one fluorophore each, thus representing one γ-secretase complex per spot.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Nearest-neighbor analysis of NCT KO MEFs rescued with both NCT-SNAP and NCT-GFP demonstrated a close to random distribution.
source: Nearest-neighbor analysis demonstrated a close to random distribution, underscoring an essentially monomeric distribution of NCT molecules at the cell surface (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Photobleaching steps of GFP-PSEN1 showed that monomeric spots are the most abundant (30% to 35%), followed by dimeric units (22% to 30%).
source: Both approaches showed that the monomeric spots are the most abundant (30% to 35%), followed by dimeric units (22% to 30%), whereas higher complexes (trimers and above) are more rarely observed.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Photon counting the number of fluorescent emitters of NCT-YFP showed that monomeric spots are the most abundant (30% to 35%), followed by dimeric units (22% to 30%).
source: Both approaches showed that the monomeric spots are the most abundant (30% to 35%), followed by dimeric units (22% to 30%), whereas higher complexes (trimers and above) are more rarely observed.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The histogram of tKO NCT-GFP/GFP-PSEN1 MEFs showed a pronounced shoulder at twice the intensity of a single GFP that disappeared at the end of movie acquisition.
source: The histogram of tKO NCT-GFP/GFP-PSEN1 MEFs showed a pronounced shoulder at twice the intensity of a single GFP that disappeared at the end of movie acquisition, meaning that the distribution shifted from complexes with one or two intact GFP tags to only one remaining GFP tag.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The distribution of spot intensities in sKO GFP-PSEN1 MEFs was similar at the beginning and the end of the movie.
source: In contrast, the distribution of spot intensities in sKO GFP-PSEN1 MEFs was similar at the beginning and the end of the movie.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The histogram of spot intensities from NCT-GFP/GFP-PSEN1 MEFs yields 42% of spots with two functional GFP and 58% with one functional GFP.
source: The histogram of spot intensities from NCT-GFP/GFP-PSEN1 MEFs yields 42% of spots with two functional GFP and 58% with one functional GFP.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The majority of PSEN1/γ-secretase complexes are mono- or dimeric complexes under both fixed and live conditions.
source: Taking the different independent approaches together, our data indicate that under both fixed and live conditions, the majority of PSEN1/γ-secretase complexes are mono- or dimeric complexes, but not higher-order clusters.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on the experimental data presented in Figure 2.

claim: On average, PSEN1/γ-secretase showed anomalous motility (mean α = 0.844).
source: On average, PSEN1/γ-secretase showed anomalous motility (mean α = 0.844) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: When classifying individual tracks, most of them have a predominant directed motility mixed with other types of motility.
source: However, when classifying individual tracks, most of them have a predominant directed motility mixed with other types of motility (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The average diffusion coefficient of PSEN1/γ-secretase is 0.15 µm/s².
source: This revealed an average diffusion coefficient of 0.15 µm/s² for PSEN1/γ-secretase (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Most of the PSEN1/γ-secretase tracks are mobile (87%) with a small fraction being immobile.
source: Further analysis showed that most of the tracks are mobile (87%) with a small fraction being immobile (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Exposure to GSI did not affect the MSD, diffusion coefficient or the overall distribution of Log10 D.
source: Exposure to GSI did not affect the MSD, diffusion coefficient or the overall distribution of Log10 D (Figure 3A–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A-E.

claim: A slight increase of the immobile fraction was found upon DAPT treatment.
source: We only found a slight increase of the immobile fraction upon DAPT treatment visible in the Log10 histogram showing the diffusion coefficient of individual tracks (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The apparent 'enrichment' of tracks at the cell edge tended to correlate with an increased number of mobile tracks.
source: The apparent 'enrichment' of tracks at the cell edge tended to correlate with an increased number of mobile tracks (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: GSI treatment mildly reduced the distribution of mobile tracks at the cell edges.
source: Our analysis thus suggests a higher presence of PSEN1/γ-secretase in the protruding or migrating edges of the cell and GSI treatment mildly reduced the distribution of mobile tracks at these edges.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The size of hotspots became significantly reduced following treatment with GSIs.
source: Interestingly, the size (Figure 3I), but not the average number of hotspots (Figure 3K), became significantly reduced following treatment with GSIs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3I.

claim: The localizations per hotspot showed a diminishing trend following treatment with GSIs.
source: In addition, the localizations per hotspot showed a diminishing trend (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Fewer tracks were found per hotspot in GSI-treated cells.
source: When examining the number of tracks per hotspot, fewer tracks were found, explaining the smaller hotspot area in GSI-treated cells (Figure 3L).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3L.

claim: Locking PSEN1/γ-secretase conformation in an active-mimicking conformation restricts visiting hotspots.
source: These data suggest that locking PSEN1/γ-secretase conformation in an active-mimicking conformation restricts visiting these hotspots.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data, representing speculation about the mechanism.

claim: Nearest-neighbor analysis demonstrated a significant association of PSEN1/γ-secretase with APP below a 100 nm distance.
source: Despite the lower density of endogenous APP at the cell surface, nearest-neighbor analysis demonstrated a significant association of PSEN1/γ-secretase with both substrates below a 100 nm distance, supporting in situ association with substrates (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Nearest-neighbor analysis demonstrated a significant association of PSEN1/γ-secretase with N-cadherin below a 100 nm distance.
source: Despite the lower density of endogenous APP at the cell surface, nearest-neighbor analysis demonstrated a significant association of PSEN1/γ-secretase with both substrates below a 100 nm distance, supporting in situ association with substrates (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Nearest-neighbor analysis of ADAM10 and PSEN1/γ-secretase showed almost no difference compared to a random distribution.
source: In contrast to substrates, nearest-neighbor analysis showed almost no difference compared to a random distribution analysis of the same spots (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Only a small fraction of ADAM10 (6% ± 0.4) showed association with PSEN1/γ-secretase.
source: Only a small fraction of ADAM10 (6% ± 0.4) showed association with PSEN1/γ-secretase.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Nearest-neighbor analysis of BACE1 and PSEN1/γ-secretase showed almost no difference compared to a random distribution.
source: In contrast to substrates, nearest-neighbor analysis showed almost no difference compared to a random distribution analysis of the same spots (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Quantitative super-resolution microscopy does not overall support the association of sheddases with PSEN1/γ-secretase in long-lived megadalton complexes.
source: This is surprising as recent biochemical evidence pointed to the association of these sheddases with PSEN1/γ-secretase in long-lived megadalton (>5 MDa) complexes (Chen et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2019). Quantitative super-resolution microscopy, however, does not overall support this.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data, representing an inference that contradicts prior biochemical findings.

claim: Hotspots of ADAM10 and BACE1 did not overlap with those of PSEN1/γ-secretase as shown by the very low Pearson's and Mander's coefficient.
source: However, hotspots of sheddases did not overlap with those of PSEN1/γ-secretase as shown by the very low Pearson's and Mander's coefficient (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: PSEN1/γ-secretase tracks associated with BACE1 hotspots had high diffusion coefficients (D = 0.08 ± 0.01 µm²/s).
source: Although there is a tendency of more PSEN1/γ-secretase tracks being associated with BACE1 hotspots (Figure 5E), they had high diffusion coefficients (D = 0.08 ± 0.01 µm²/s), indicating that these tracks represent PSEN1/γ-secretase merely passing by BACE1 hotspots without actually being associated to it (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: PSEN1/γ-secretase tracks that frequent ADAM10 hotspots have decreased diffusion coefficients (D = 0.04 ± 0.02 µm²/s).
source: On the contrary, PSEN1/γ-secretase tracks that frequent ADAM10 hotspots have decreased diffusion coefficients (D = 0.04 ± 0.02 µm²/s, Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: PSEN1/γ-secretase tracks with decreased diffusion coefficients at ADAM10 hotspots may represent complexes that are slowing down to associate with ADAM10-frequented regions.
source: These tracks may, therefore, represent complexes that are slowing down to associate with ADAM10-frequented regions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data, representing speculation about the mechanism.

claim: PSEN1/γ-secretase and ADAM10 may frequent common nanodomains at the PM.
source: As our nearest-neighbor analysis could not support significant close or direct associations, an alternative explanation might be that PSEN1/γ-secretase and ADAM10 frequent common nanodomains at the PM, the nature of which remains to be investigated.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data, representing speculation about an alternative explanation.

claim: This is the first time that PSEN1/γ-secretase stoichiometry is demonstrated in situ.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first time that PSEN1/γ-secretase stoichiometry is demonstrated in situ.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings in the context of the field.

claim: The existence of dimeric γ-secretase complexes is consistent with earlier biochemical evidence.
source: The latter is consistent with earlier biochemical evidence on the existence of dimeric complexes (Hébert et al., 2003; Cervantes et al., 2004) as well as in lower resolution structures (Ogura et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hébert et al., 2003; Cervantes et al., 2004; Ogura et al., 2006.

claim: When analyzed by blue native PAGE, mostly a ~ 440 kDa complex is reported possibly coinciding with a dimeric configuration.
source: When analyzed by blue native PAGE, mostly a ~ 440 kDa complex is reported possible coinciding with a dimeric configuration as the sum of the four components is about 210 kDa (Kimberly et al., 2003; Fraering et al., 2004; Spasic et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kimberly et al., 2003; Fraering et al., 2004; Spasic et al., 2007.

claim: SIM analysis on PM sheets achieves single-molecule imaging.
source: From a technical perspective, the fact that we can image PSEN1/γ-secretase as single complexes implicates that SIM analysis on PM sheets achieves single-molecule imaging, likely because imaging PM monolayers increases the signal to noise ratio.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the technical capabilities demonstrated in the study.

claim: Diffusion coefficients of membrane proteins range typically from ~0.0002 to 0.5 µm²/s using single-particle tracking methods.
source: Diffusion coefficients of membrane proteins range typically from ~0.0002 to 0.5 µm²/s using single-particle tracking methods.
evidence: This is general knowledge about membrane protein diffusion.

claim: PSEN1/γ-secretase complexes have a mean diffusion coefficient of 0.15 µm²/s, which is fast for a complex with twenty transmembrane domains.
source: SptPALM revealed very dynamic PSEN1/γ-secretase complexes with a mean diffusion coefficient of 0.15 µm²/s, which is fast for a complex with twenty transmembrane domains (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and represents an interpretation of the significance of this value.

claim: CFTR diffuses extremely slow (0.005 µm²/s).
source: Other multimembrane proteins like cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) diffuse extremely slow (0.005 µm²/s)
evidence: This is general knowledge about CFTR diffusion used for comparison.

claim: G-protein coupled receptors have low mean diffusion coefficients (0.05–0.06 µm²/s for GABA and β1/β2-adrenergic receptors).
source: whereas G-protein coupled receptors, that also di-/oligomerize at the cell surface, have as well low mean diffusion coefficients (0.05–0.06 µm²/s for GABA and β1/β2-adrenergic receptors [Bates et al., 2006; Calebiro et al., 2013]).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bates et al., 2006 and Calebiro et al., 2013.

claim: Rhodopsin has a diffusion coefficient of 0.77 µm²/s.
source: Only rhodopsin and smoothened, both seven transmembrane domain proteins, have much higher coefficients (0.77 µm²/s and 0.26 µm²/s, respectively) (Milenkovic et al., 2015; Kreutzberger et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Milenkovic et al., 2015 and Kreutzberger et al., 2019.

claim: Smoothened has a diffusion coefficient of 0.26 µm²/s.
source: Only rhodopsin and smoothened, both seven transmembrane domain proteins, have much higher coefficients (0.77 µm²/s and 0.26 µm²/s, respectively) (Milenkovic et al., 2015; Kreutzberger et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Milenkovic et al., 2015 and Kreutzberger et al., 2019.

claim: Rhomboids diffuse extremely fast with a mean diffusion coefficient of 0.88 µm²/s.
source: Interestingly, rhomboids, another member of the i-CLiP family, diffuse extremely fast with a mean diffusion coefficient of 0.88 µm²/s (Kreutzberger et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kreutzberger et al., 2019.

claim: The mechanism behind rhomboid fast diffusion appears to be a hydrophobic mismatch with the surrounding lipids, causing a membrane distortion that reduces membrane viscosity.
source: The mechanism behind this appears to be a hydrophobic mismatch with the surrounding lipids, causing a membrane distortion that reduces in turn membrane viscosity.
evidence: This is general knowledge about rhomboid diffusion mechanisms.

claim: Diffusion is the rate-limiting step in substrate catalysis for rhomboids.
source: As diffusion is the rate-limiting step in substrate catalysis, rhomboids overcame this by breaking the viscosity imposed 'speed limit' to facilitate substrate processing.
evidence: This is general knowledge about rhomboid catalysis.

claim: PSEN1/γ-secretase has a tendency to be more mobile at the cell's edges.
source: PSEN1/γ-secretase has a tendency to be more mobile at the cell's edges, where it is assumed to be more active/required because of the higher presence and turnover of adhesion molecules (Haapasalo and Kovacs, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G and citation to Haapasalo and Kovacs, 2011.

claim: PSEN1 has been reported to interact with filamin, an actin-binding protein.
source: For instance, PSEN1 has been reported to interact with filamin, an actin-binding protein (Zhang et al., 1998; Guo et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zhang et al., 1998 and Guo et al., 2000.

claim: Absence of the orthologous PSEN in the moss Physcomitrella patens causes cytoskeletal defects.
source: More indirectly, absence of the orthologous PSEN in the moss Physcomitrella patens, causes cytoskeletal defects pointing to a scaffolding role of the moss PSEN between the cytoskeleton and adherent proteins (Khandelwal et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Khandelwal et al., 2007.

claim: Anchoring to the cytoskeleton usually results in an immobile state as shown for CD44 and integrin β1 and β2.
source: Anchoring to the cytoskeleton usually results in an immobile state as shown for CD44 and integrin β1 and β2 (Rossier et al., 2012; Freeman et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rossier et al., 2012 and Freeman et al., 2018.

claim: Confined motility of α2-macroglobulin receptor (α2MR) and transferrin receptor (TfR) has been related to the enclosure of the protein in between actin filaments of the cytoskeleton.
source: Confined motility of α2-macroglobulin receptor (α2MR) and transferrin receptor (TfR) has been related to the enclosure of the protein in between actin filaments of the cytoskeleton, leading to the 'picket-fence' hypothesis (Kusumi et al., 1993; Sako and Kusumi, 1994).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kusumi et al., 1993 and Sako and Kusumi, 1994.

claim: In the AMPAR, conformational changes triggered by binding of glutamate leads to a desensitized state correspondent to a switch from immobile to mobile molecules.
source: In the AMPAR, conformational changes triggered by binding of glutamate leads to a desensitized state correspondent to a switch from immobile to mobile molecules (Constals et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Constals et al., 2015.

source: Although experimental and simulated data show that PSEN1/γ-secretase also undergoes conformational changes upon substrate binding or in the presence of inhibitors (Bai et al., 2015a; Aguayo-Ortiz and Dominguez, 2018; Yang et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citations to Bai et al., 2015a; Aguayo-Ortiz and Dominguez, 2018; Yang et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2019.

source: The support for the megadalton-sized complexes concept is majorly biochemical in nature and based on the void fractions of gel filtration-based separations of crude detergent extracts.
evidence: This is a statement about the nature of prior evidence for megadalton complexes.

source: Thus, it cannot be excluded that such macrocomplexes may be formed during or after extraction.
evidence: This is speculation about an alternative explanation for prior biochemical findings.

source: Our single-particle analysis rather favors the idea of a 1:1 encountering of PSEN1/γ-secretase to areas where sheddases reside to 'accept' the respective substrate CTF for further processing.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data, representing an inference about the mechanism.

source: At most, this would result in short temporal or transient associations via substrate transfer.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data, representing speculation about the nature of the associations.

claim: The presented single-molecule resolution analyses uncovered the distribution and dynamics of PSEN1/γ-secretase at the PM.
source: In conclusion, the presented single-molecule resolution analyses uncovered the distribution and dynamics of PSEN1/γ-secretase at the PM
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's findings.

claim: The study shows, for the first time, the stoichiometry of the γ-secretase complex while embedded in its natural environment.
source: In conclusion, the presented single-molecule resolution analyses uncovered the distribution and dynamics of PSEN1/γ-secretase at the PM, as well as show, for the first time, the stoichiometry of the complex while embedded in its natural environment.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's findings.

claim: Single-molecule resolution approaches will become a standard in the field to further decipher the dynamics of intramembrane proteolysis.
source: We anticipate that single-molecule resolution approaches will become a standard in the field to further decipher the dynamics of intramembrane proteolysis particularly in the neuron.
evidence: This is speculation about the future impact of the methodological approaches used in the study.

claim: Many γ-secretase substrates are adhesion proteins functioning in axonal outgrowth and synapse formation and stability.
source: Herein, the distribution and dynamics of these enzymes at the growth cone and synapse will be of particular interest given that many γ-secretase substrates are adhesion proteins functioning in axonal outgrowth and synapse formation and stability (Jurisch-Yaksi et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jurisch-Yaksi et al., 2013.

claim: Synaptic plasticity is affected in absence of PSENs and in PSEN1 FAD models.
source: In an Alzheimer's disease context, synaptic plasticity is affected in absence of PSENs and in PSEN1 FAD models (Saura et al., 2004; Priller et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Saura et al., 2004 and Priller et al., 2007.
